title: Entities, Components and Systems
summary: How should a game represent its thousands of objects? Deep inheritance trees (`Monster : Character : Entity`) become rigid and slow. Many engines use **entity-component-system** (ECS) design instead: an **entity** is just an id, **components** are plain data attached to it, and **systems** are loops over every entity with a given set of components. This lesson explains why, and builds a small ECS on the **sparse set** structure.
markdown:
## The trouble with deep hierarchies

The object-oriented first attempt at a game world looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    E["Entity"] --> C["Character"]
    E --> P["Prop"]
    C --> PL["Player"]
    C --> M["Monster"]
    M --> F["FlyingMonster"]
    P --> B["Barrel"]
```

Then the designers ask for a barrel that can fly, a monster that can be picked up like a prop, and a player who can turn into a barrel. Each request fits awkwardly into the tree, and features drift up into the base class until `Entity` has a hundred members, most unused by most objects. Performance suffers too: each object is a separate heap allocation with a vptr, updating them means a virtual call each, and their data is scattered (lessons 3.02, 3.05).

## Composition: entities, components, systems

ECS splits things differently:

| Part | Is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Entity** | An id. Nothing else. | `Entity{ 42 }` |
| **Component** | A small, plain struct of data, attached to an entity | `Position{ x, y }`, `Velocity{ vx, vy }`, `Health{ hp }`, `Sprite{ textureId }` |
| **System** | A function that loops over every entity having certain components | Movement: every entity with Position **and** Velocity |

A flying barrel is just an entity with `Position`, `Velocity`, `Sprite` and `Breakable`. A monster you can pick up has `Carryable` added. No class hierarchy has to change: behaviour comes from which components an entity has, and which systems act on them.

```cpp
void movementSystem(World& world, float dt)
{
    for (Entity e : world.with<Position, Velocity>())
    {
        Position& p{ world.get<Position>(e) };
        const Velocity& v{ world.get<Velocity>(e) };
        p.x += v.vx * dt;
        p.y += v.vy * dt;
    }
}
```

## Why it is fast

Each component type is stored in its own **dense array**: all `Position`s side by side, all `Velocity`s side by side. A system walks those arrays in order, which is exactly what caches and vectorisation want (lessons 2.07, 7.09): no pointer chasing, no virtual calls, every byte loaded is used. This layout is called **data-oriented design**, and it is the main reason large engines adopted ECS.

## The sparse set

How do you store components so that you can (a) loop over all of them densely, (b) find an entity's component instantly, and (c) add and remove them cheaply? The usual answer is a **sparse set** per component type:

```
sparse: indexed by entity id → position in the dense arrays (or "none")
        [0]: none   [1]: 0   [2]: none   [3]: 2   [4]: 1

dense:  entity ids in order       [1]  [4]  [3]
        components, same order    {P1} {P4} {P3}
```

| Operation | How | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Does entity e have it? | `sparse[e] != none` | Constant |
| Get e's component | `components[sparse[e]]` | Constant |
| Add to e | Append to the dense arrays; `sparse[e] = new index` | Constant (amortised) |
| Remove from e | Swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): move the last element into e's slot, fix the moved entity's sparse entry | Constant |
| Loop over all | Walk the dense arrays | Fast, contiguous |

It combines lesson 3.07's swap-and-pop with lesson 3.10's stable ids. The practice task builds one.

## Systems that need several components

`world.with<Position, Velocity>()` must find entities that have **both**. With sparse sets, loop over the **smaller** of the two sets and check the other with a constant-time lookup. Larger engines group entities by their exact set of components into **archetypes**, each stored as its own table, so every system's loop is a straight walk with no checks; that is how Unity's DOTS and the `flecs` library work. `EnTT`, a popular open-source C++ ECS, is built on sparse sets.

## When not to use ECS

ECS shines with many similar objects and simple, repeated behaviour. For a game with a few dozen unique objects, or for one-off logic (a boss's scripted sequence, the user interface), plain classes are simpler and fine. Many shipped games mix both: an ECS for the crowd, ordinary objects for the rest.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Putting logic in components
> Components are data. Behaviour lives in systems.

> [!warning] Keeping pointers to components
> Removing another entity's component can move this one (swap-and-pop). Store the entity id and look the component up.

> [!warning] Adding or removing components while a system loops over them
> The arrays change under the loop. Queue structural changes and apply them after the system finishes.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What are entities, components and systems?
- Entities are classes, components are their virtual functions, systems are their base classes
+ Entities are ids; components are plain data attached to entities; systems are functions processing every entity with a given set of components
- Entities are files, components are folders, systems are the build tools
- Entities are threads, components are locks, systems are queues
> An entity has no behaviour of its own: what it is comes from which components it has.

? What problem with deep inheritance does ECS solve?
- That inheritance cannot be used with templates
- That virtual functions cannot be called from other threads
- That classes cannot have more than one constructor
+ Rigid hierarchies, and scattered virtual-heavy memory
> Composition lets any entity have any mix of components, and systems loop over tightly packed arrays.

? What does a sparse set store, and why?
+ An id-to-index array plus dense arrays, for O(1) changes and fast loops
- A hash table from entity names to components, for fast lookup by name
- A linked list of components, so removal never moves anything
- One array per entity listing its components, so systems can find them
> Removal swaps the last dense element into the gap and fixes the sparse entry, which keeps it constant time.

? In ECS, what is an entity?
- A class with virtual functions
+ Just an id that components are attached to
- A system
> All its data lives in components; all behaviour in systems.

? Why are ECS systems often faster than looping over objects with virtual `update` functions?
- Systems run on the GPU
- Components are smaller than objects
+ They walk contiguous plain data with no virtual calls
> Data-oriented layout suits caches and vectorisation.

? In a sparse set, how is a component removed in constant time?
+ Swap-and-pop, then fix the moved entity's entry
- All later components are shifted down
- The slot is marked empty and skipped
> The dense arrays stay dense.
```
ideas:
- Sketch the components you would give: a player, a homing missile, a treasure chest, and a torch on a wall.
- Write `movementSystem` for a world stored as plain `std::vector<Position>` and `std::vector<Velocity>` with matching indices, and time it on a million entities.
- Look at the README of the EnTT library on GitHub and find its sparse-set documentation.
